what_this_is: The per-check AXIS DECOMPOSITION for the OC checks C1a's crosswalk lands an edge on and A3 did NOT decompose. A3 committed 13 of the 175; its scope block hands the other 162 to C1. This file holds C1a's, C1b-i's, C1b-ii's, C1b-iii's, C1c-i's, C1c-ii's and C1c-iii's share of them and nothing else. (The enumeration in this field had gone STALE: it named C1a, C1b-i and C1b-ii only, and was already wrong at C1b-iii's commit and wrong again at C1c-i's. `owner` and `scope.population` were both kept current while this one was not, which is what a third copy of one fact costs. Corrected by C1c-ii rather than dropped, and named in its close-out so it does not read as having always been right; C1c-iii extends all three together for the same reason.)
why_a_second_file_and_not_an_edit_of_A3s: Editing docs/conformance/oc-axes-2026-07-28.json would give one artefact two owners — the MES-24 two-censuses defect, where the two disagree and nothing detects it. A3 owns its 13; C1 owns what C1 extracts. Disjointness is ASSERTED BY THE BUILDER (mix conformance.crosswalk refuses on any overlap), not left to a convention. PM-ratified as D4, MES-97 comment 27858.
axis_source_rule: AXES COME FROM THE PREDICATE, NEVER FROM THE DESCRIPTION — docs/conformance/match-relation.md §2, cited not restated.
difference_from_A3s_13: A3's 13 are all `a(...)`-form checks whose predicate is an inline arrow function, so every axis expression is a substring of the emitting excerpt itself. NONE of the checks here is like that: every one computes its predicate into a minified binding BEFORE the emitting call, and three of them are decided at a site that is not the emitting site at all. C1b-ii's 9 are the sharpest case — their verdict is `i.length===0` / `o.length===0` over an error accumulator filled by a ternary several hundred bytes earlier, so EVERY axis expr lives in a `context_excerpts` entry and none in the evaluator excerpt. So each row carries `context_excerpts` — further addressed spans the predicate depends on — and an axis `expr` is a verbatim substring of the evaluator excerpt OR of one of them. The row says which, in `expr_found_in`.

provenance.emitting_spans_from: docs/conformance/oc-emitting-sites-2026-07-28.json — generated by mix conformance.locator, not re-cut by hand
provenance.context_spans_from: located by unique-substring search against the same build; each is unique in it
provenance.bytes_are_not_stored_here: Spans only. `mix conformance.crosswalk` lifts the bytes LIVE from the build at these spans and refuses if any axis `expr` is not a verbatim substring of what it lifted. Storing the bytes here as well would create a second copy that can drift from the build without anything noticing — the same reasoning bucket-0 gives for lifting rather than remembering.

polarity_rule: `pass_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the passing arm. `fail_when_true` — the expression being TRUE is the failing arm. Read off the branch the excerpt actually writes, never off the requirement's wording.
preconditions_rule: A list of `{guard, kind, on_failure, reads}`. A precondition is NOT an axis, and the reason is NOT the status it writes: it is that the guard reads something OTHER than a behaviour of the implementation under test — the harness's own transport, whether a diagnostic tool is listed, whether the probe was run at all — so an ET claim can neither agree with it nor contradict it, and `shape_from_axes/1` never sees one. C1a stated the rule as `its failure makes the check not evaluate (SKIPPED)`, and C1c-i measured that that is NOT what the artefacts do: A3's own server-stateless rows record `()=>n?` and `()=>S?` and `!r||!i` as preconditions whose `on_failure` is an ERROR MESSAGE, and the check goes red. Three `on_failure` shapes occur in this file and each is written as what it is — `SKIPPED` (ServerIdentifiesInResultMeta's `if(_)return{skipped:!0`, and the two `listChanged` rows' capability guards), a FAILURE naming the probe, and a WARNING carrying `details:{untestable:!0}`. The rule as C1a wrote it would have forced a dozen harness-transport guards to be recorded as AXES, and every ET claim would then have been `silent` on them — which makes every red-OC edge `:partial` and bucket 4b by construction, and would have made A3 §3's `(red, green, :full)` escalation UNREACHABLE on the first leg where it can occur. Restating the rule on its actual ground is therefore not a loosening; it is what stops the decomposition deciding an adjudication.

scope.how_the_18_were_cut: The method, stated once here because C1c-ii/iii/iv inherit it. START at the locator's `emitting_byte_span` for the row — never at a grep. WIDEN to the enclosing balanced expression, which for these rows the locator has already done: 15 of the 18 are `rung: id_literal_pair` pinned at level `row` with a single site, and the three RequestMetaInvalid rows are `id_template_prefix` pinned at level `loop`, where one site emits three rows. READ the axes off the branch the excerpt WRITES: one axis per conjunct of the deciding test, `expr` verbatim, polarity from the arm that carries `error` rather than from the requirement's wording. Where the predicate reads a name bound OUTSIDE the excerpt, locate the binding by UNIQUE SUBSTRING search and record it as a `context_excerpts` entry with the reason it is needed — every context span in the 18 was located that way and each is unique in the build. NOTHING here stores bytes: the generator lifts them live under `--harness` and refuses any `expr`, `guard` or listed conjunct that is not a verbatim substring of what it lifted.
scope.what_the_18_cost_against_the_client_leg: Lighter per row than CG7's 29, and measured rather than assumed: CG7 needed FOUR `locator_row_rejected` rows and 24 rows carrying `check_id_found_in`, because its ids are computed from argument values. All 18 here are `locator_row` — not one rejects the locator's span — and only the three RequestMetaInvalid rows need anything beyond the default id location. (C1c-i) The 18 yield 26 axes; CG7's 29 yielded 47.
scope.the_thirty_six_C1c_ii_adds: The MRTR / input-required-result family (SEP-2322, server side): 22 SUBSTANTIVE checks over 14 scenarios, plus 14 `WireSchemaValid` rows — one per scenario, all emitted from ONE site, and each decomposed because G19 requires a declared check to be read before it can be reported in bucket 2. (C1c-ii) Two shapes recur and both are stated on the rows rather than here: eleven checks fill an ERROR ACCUMULATOR whose emptiness is the verdict, so every axis lives in a `context_excerpts` entry and none at the emitting site (the C1b-ii shape); three compute a BOOLEAN FLAG from a `&&` chain instead, and the conjuncts of that chain are the axes. How many axes each yields was read at the build, not assumed: the family's 36 rows carry 97 axes and 43 preconditions between them.
scope.what_the_36_cost_against_the_18: Measured, not assumed. C1c-i's 18 rows yielded 26 axes; C1c-ii's 36 yield 97 — 2.7 axes a row against 1.4, and the reason is visible in the shapes: `server-stateless` is mostly one- and two-axis checks decided at the emitting site, while this family decides on an error accumulator filled by a five- or nine-arm chain. The DIRECTION is the opposite of the member count: this slice is member-light (5, against C1c-i's 59) and axis-heavy. Neither figure predicts the other, which is why the ticket was sized on checks and the member count was measured rather than inferred.
scope.what_C1c_iii_contributes_and_the_shape_i: (C1c-iii) 41 rows carrying 107 axes, and the 41 are NOT 41 independent readings. NINETEEN of them are `WireSchemaValid` — one per declared scenario, all at the single generic validator span [325368,325721], one axis each. (C1c-iii) The TWENTY-TWO substantive rows carry the other 88. So the axis work of this slice is 22 readings, and the row count is what A1's six-field key makes of one of them. Stated here because `41 rows` and `41 decompositions` are different quantities and the first is the one the arithmetic uses.
scope.what_C1c_iv_contributes_and_why_it_is_th:
TWELVE rows carrying 21 axes, and they close the decomposition: after C1c-iv-a the locator's 173 keys are exhausted between A3's file and this one. (C1c-iv-a) The shape is unlike every slice before it, and the reason is that these three scenarios are the only SERVER scenarios whose checks are not emitted at their own decision site.

SEVEN of the twelve decide somewhere the locator does not point. The five `*CachingHints` rows are `rung: id_literal_pair` pinned at row level onto an `i(...)` CALL that names the check and the endpoint and carries no `status:` whatever: the status ternary and both predicates live in the shared `nr` builder the call returns through, addressed as `context:caching_hint_verdict`. The two DNS rows are pinned onto an OBJECT LITERAL — id, name, description, timestamp, specReferences — whose status is attached later by spread at a predicate several hundred bytes away. In all seven cases the locator's span is correct as a LOCATION and useless as an EVALUATOR, and an axis read off it alone could only have been read off the description, which `axis_source_rule` forbids. This is why the `how_the_18_were_cut` method's first step — START at the locator's span, never at a grep — is followed by a second step, and this slice is where the second step does all the work.

ONE of the twelve has TWO emitting sites for one check id, and the choice between them is a MEASUREMENT rather than a reading: `ServerSSEStreamsFunctional` is pushed from a `g>0` arm with a three-way ternary and from a `g===0` arm with a hard-coded `status:`INFO``, and the accepted run's 2 SUCCESS / 0 INFO is what settles which fired. The row records that reasoning on itself.

TWO of the twelve carry a NON-VACUITY axis that the check's own description does not mention — `TtlNonNegative` and `CacheScopeValid` each red when NO endpoint returned the field they range over. Without that limb a server returning no caching hints at all would pass a check named `All ttlMs values are non-negative integers` by quantifying over the empty set. It is an axis because it is a predicate in the ladder, not because it is in the wording.

checks.emitting_span_provenance_why: The locator names THREE sites for this row's key and its own `rung_pin_level` is `check`, not `row` — the name is computed at the site (`ClientMcpMethodHeader_${n.replace(/\//g,`_`)}`), so the six Method rows share one site and the three Name rows another. The span taken here is one the locator names, which is what `locator_row` asserts and all G18 checks; WHICH of the three it is, is this row's reading and not the locator's authority. Stated because a check-level pin cannot distinguish the Method push from the Name push, and G18 would accept either against either row.

axes.expr: i.push(`Missing Mcp-Method header on ${n} request. Clients MUST include the Mcp-Method header on all POST requests.`)
axes.polarity_reading: the ELSE arm of `r?r!==n&&i.push(...):i.push(...)` — reached when `r`, the `mcp-method` header, is falsy, and it pushes an error; the push's `status:i.length===0?`SUCCESS`:`FAILURE`` then makes a non-empty accumulator the failure
axes.requires: every POST carries an `Mcp-Method` header — SEP-2243's MUST, as the pushed message itself states

axes.polarity_reading: `r?r!==n&&i.push(...)` — inside the header-present arm, inequality with the body method `n` pushes an error. `!==` is case-sensitive, which the pushed message says in as many words
axes.requires: the header's value is the body's `method`, byte-for-byte and case-sensitively

axes.requires: that same unrelated tools/call carries no `requestState`

checks.conjunction_note: TWO axes, and they are not one behaviour spelled twice: `inputResponses` and `requestState` are separate fields written by separate code paths, and a client that leaked one without the other fails exactly one of the two pushes. Grouping them would hide a real partial.

key: Client MUST assume resultType "complete" when not specified
checks.emitting_span_provenance_why: ACCEPTED, with the residual stated on the row rather than left to be found. The locator pins this row at level CHECK, not ROW — the id reaches the site through the binding `i` — and it names FOUR sites for it. Two are this check's own pushes (the FAILURE arm at [348629, 348940] and the SUCCESS arm at [349056, 349247]); the other two are unrelated code that merely binds some `i` (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(i,`requestState`)` at [535065, 535119] and `f.join(i,`.git`)` at [770581, 770597]). G18 would have accepted either of those two against this row, so the acceptance is weaker than it looks and is said so. The span taken is the FAILURE arm because it is the arm the predicate decides; the SUCCESS arm is addressed as a context excerpt so the polarity is read off both branches; and the id LITERAL is at NEITHER push, which is why `check_id_found_in` names the guard excerpt instead.

context_excerpts.label: result_type_guard
context_excerpts.why: THE PREDICATE AND THE ID LITERAL ARE BOTH HERE — `let i=`sep-2322-default-result-type-complete`;if(t){`. Both pushes write their `status` as a constant, so a reader who follows the locator to a push and stops finds no predicate at all: the S9-16 shape, second instance

context_excerpts.label: success_arm
context_excerpts.why: the other arm of the same `if`, addressed so the polarity is read off both branches and not off one

axes.polarity_reading: `if(t){ ... status:`FAILURE`, errorMessage:`Client retried with inputResponses even though the result had no resultType (should default to complete)` ... return}` followed by the unguarded `status:`SUCCESS`` push — `t` TRUE is the failing arm
axes.requires: a result carrying no `resultType` is read as `complete`, so the client returns it to the caller and does NOT retry with `inputResponses`

checks.emitting_site_is_not_the_predicate: Both pushes write their `status` as a LITERAL. The verdict is the `if(t)` 125 bytes earlier, and the FAILURE arm additionally splices any already-recorded row for this id out of `checks` before pushing — so the result is decided, and any earlier result for it erased, at a site the locator does not name as this row's.

key: Every JSON-RPC message the implementation sent is valid per the spec JSON schema for the negotiated spec version

context_excerpts.label: implementation_violation_filter
context_excerpts.why: THE PREDICATE IS THE FILTER. `o` — the accumulator the emitting site reads as `o.length===0` — is `t.filter(e=>e.origin===`implementation`)`, so what the check scores is not `were there violations` but `were there violations ATTRIBUTED TO THE IMPLEMENTATION`

context_excerpts.label: evaluability_gate
context_excerpts.why: holds the early `return[]` that decides whether this check is emitted at all

context_excerpts.label: harness_origin_sibling
context_excerpts.why: the `origin===`harness`` sibling, addressed so the SCOPE of this check is evidence and not inference: violations in messages the HARNESS sent are scored by `WireSchemaHarnessError`, never here

axes.polarity_reading: `o=t.filter(e=>e.origin===`implementation`)` then `status:o.length===0?`SUCCESS`:`FAILURE`` — a violation whose origin is the implementation is what fails it
axes.requires: every JSON-RPC message OUR side put on the wire validates against the published spec schema for the negotiated version

checks.scope_note: ONE DIRECTION ONLY, and that is why this row carries the `harness_origin_sibling` excerpt. The filter scopes the check to messages the IMPLEMENTATION SENT. Nothing here scores what the implementation does with a message it RECEIVED — those violations carry `origin===`harness``, go to `WireSchemaHarnessError`, and that check is a bug report about the harness rather than a score of our parsing. An ET claim about DECODING an inbound message is therefore silent on this axis by the SHAPE of the check, not by a reading of it — and C1b-iii's bucket-1 records for the inbound decoders rest on this excerpt.

preconditions.reads: whether any message was observed at all; a run that validated nothing emits no check rather than a vacuous SUCCESS

checks.two_site_note: TWO sites, and the locator names both. They are ALTERNATIVES, not halves: the summary site is written `r.some(e=>e.id===`sep-2575-http-server-error-jsonrpc-id`)||r.push({...})`, so it emits ONLY IF the helper has not already pushed. The accepted run's status for this key is SUCCESS, so the row that was actually emitted came from the SUMMARY site, and that is the span this decomposition records as `emitting_byte_span`. The helper is recorded as a context excerpt because the PREDICATE lives there and nowhere else — recording the summary alone would decompose a counter and call it a requirement. This is the `DefaultResultTypeComplete` shape from C1b-iii, one leg further: there the two pushes were literals and the decision was at an `if`; here the two pushes are a literal and a ternary and the decision is at a helper several hundred bytes away.

checks.why_the_two_early_returns_are_axes: `preconditions_rule` is applied and it puts them on the axis side, which is worth stating because their MESSAGES say `Prerequisite failed`. The rule's ground is not the status a guard writes but WHAT IT READS: a precondition reads something other than a behaviour of the implementation under test. Both of these read the implementation's own round-1 response. They are also not evaluability gates — each is a `return n.push({... status:`FAILURE` ...})`, so a server that fails them is scored RED on this check rather than left unscored. Contrast the `catch` clause on the same scenario, which reads whether the harness's transport threw and IS a precondition.
checks.two_messages_one_requirement: The two pushes inside `o.error||(...)` are not two axes. They are one requirement — `the tampered retry is rejected with a JSON-RPC error` — reported with two different diagnostics depending on whether the server COMPLETED the call or merely failed to error. context_excerpts.label: sse_stream_functional_predicate
context_excerpts.why: where `v` is computed — one read per stream against a 2 s timeout, a stream counting as functional when it is not in error. context_excerpts.label: sse_streams_json_sibling
context_excerpts.why: THE OTHER EMITTING SITE OF THE SAME CHECK ID. Addressed so the choice of emitting span is evidence rather than assertion — see `why_this_row_has_two_sites_and_which_one_fired`.

axes.polarity_reading: `status:v===g?`SUCCESS`:v>0?`WARNING`:`FAILURE`` — a THREE-way ternary, and only strict equality is SUCCESS. checks.scope_note: ONE EVENT, ONE TIMEOUT, AND NOTHING ABOUT ITS CONTENT. Each stream is scored by racing a single `read()` against a 2 s timer; a `null` from the timer is NOT an error, so a stream that opens and stays silent counts as FUNCTIONAL. The event is not decoded and its payload is never compared with the `tools/list` request that opened it. The check is therefore about stream LIVENESS, not about correct SSE framing or correct results.
checks.why_this_row_has_two_sites_and_which_one: A MEASUREMENT, NOT A PREFERENCE. `server-sse-streams-functional` is pushed from two places — the `g>0` arm with the three-way ternary, and the `g===0` arm with a hard-coded `status:`INFO`` and its own description — so the locator legitimately reports two spans and the row has to choose one. It is chosen by reading the accepted run rather than by reading the code: docs/conformance/server-2026-07-28.json records this scenario as 2 SUCCESS, 0 INFO, so the INFO arm did not fire and the emitting site is the `g>0` one. Had the run recorded an INFO this row would decompose to NO axis at all, because that arm's status is a literal with no predicate over it. G18 ACCEPTS EITHER, WHICH IS WHY THE REASONING IS WRITTEN DOWN. The guard requires a `locator_row` span to be ONE OF the spans the locator names for that row's key, so for a row with two sites it cannot adjudicate the choice between them — both would pass it. This field is the compensating record, and it names the artefact that settles the choice rather than asserting the answer. `ResourcesReadCachingHints` is the other two-site row in this slice and the same residual applies to it; its own `resources_read_skip_guard` excerpt carries the equivalent note.

preconditions.reads: whether any of the three responses carried `content-type: text/event-stream`. MEASURED at the accepted run: the scenario recorded 2 SUCCESS and 0 INFO, so this arm was taken.

emitting_span_provenance_rule: Every row states where its `emitting_byte_span` came from, and the generator CHECKS the statement against MES-97's locator output (G18). `locator_row` — the span is one the locator names for this row's key, and the generator requires that. `locator_row_rejected` — the locator's own `rung_pin_level` for that row is NOT `row`, so it does not claim to pin the row; the span it names belongs to a sibling and is refused. The generator then requires the reverse: the pin level must not be `row`, the span used must NOT be one of the locator's, and a reason must be given. Four of C1b-i's 29 rows are rejections; C1a's 11 are all `locator_row`, and were so before this field existed. C1b-ii's 9 are all `locator_row` TOO, and each carries an `emitting_span_provenance_why` anyway — not because G18 demands one on an acceptance (it does not), but because the locator pins these rows at level CHECK and names three sites for every one of them, so G18 would accept the Name push against a Method row and vice versa. The acceptance is honest and the residual it leaves is stated on the row rather than in this rule. C1b-iii's 4 are all `locator_row`, and ONE of them — DefaultResultTypeComplete — is the same shape again and carries its own `emitting_span_provenance_why`: the locator pins it at level CHECK and names FOUR sites, two of which are not this check's pushes at all but unrelated code binding some `i`. Saying so on the row is the whole remedy available here; G18 cannot distinguish them, and pretending otherwise would be the AC7 error. C1c-ii's 36 are all `locator_row` and none is a rejection: every row in the family is pinned by the locator at level `row` (the id literal sits beside the row's own name at every site), so the choice among a row's sites is between an EVALUATOR site and a `catch`-arm site that carries the same id — and this file takes the evaluator site in all 36. That is a reading the locator does not make for it, and it is the same residual C1b-ii recorded for the header rows rather than a new one. C1c-iii's 41 are all `locator_row` and none is a rejection: the locator pins every row in the slice at level `row`.
